Decision 01 of 08

Market Segments

Three durable, manageable segments — entered in sequence, each chosen for a distinct demand pattern.

Construction
Year 1 — Launch | High pain
Contractors and small firms with 1–5 crews.

The sharpest pain: Owners work on-site all day while new business calls go unanswered. Each missed call can be a multi-thousand-dollar project. So willingness to pay is high and the value story is simple.

Florist
Year 2 — Expansion | Seasonal peaks
Independent florists and small shops.

Demand concentrates into brutal seasonal peaks—Valentine's Day, Mother's Day, wedding season—when every unanswered call is a lost order. A platform that absorbs surges earns its keep in a single week.

Cleaning Services
Year 2 — Expansion | Volume play
Residential and small commercial cleaning companies.

Lower ticket sizes, but high volume and strong recurrence. Winning means coordinating many recurring appointments efficiently—exactly what shared scheduling and dispatch infrastructure does well.

Why these segments stay manageable: Each segment is durable — demand for repairs, flowers, and cleaning does not disappear. Construction, Florist, and Cleaning differs not in fundamental workflows but in configuration, not in kind. Sequenced entry (Construction in Year 1, Florist and Cleaning in Year 2) lets the team prove the platform on one high-pain segment before scaling to seasonal and volume-driven models.

Decision 02 of 08

Strategic Intent

Revenue growth through two levers: entering new markets in sequence, and deepening each market with product variants.

The stated goal: Reach $2M ARR by Year 3 by pairing market entry (Construction → Florist → Cleaning) with a variant roadmap that raises revenue per customer over time.

Year 1

Enter with Construction

SkillMate AI launches with phone assistance for contractors — the highest-pain segment — and proves the core platform.

Year 2

Expand to Florist & Cleaning

The same core extends to seasonal-peak (Florist) and volume-play (Cleaning) segments through configuration and add-on variants.

Year 3

Scale variants to $2M ARR

Add-on variants — estimation, smart scheduling, seasonal assist, multi-location — deepen revenue per customer toward the stated goal.

Why variants, not new products: Each variant reuses the shared platform—AI call handling, scheduling, customer data, integrations—and adds unique logic only where a segment demands it. That keeps marginal cost per new capability low and lets revenue grow faster than engineering headcount.

One platform core carries every segment; specialization happens only at the edges.

Operator benefits: One AI engine. One customer database. One scheduling system. Training cost ↓, maintenance ↓, labor mobility ↑. Customers see a product optimized for their segment; you see a reusable platform.

Reduced training: Operators learn one system. Moving between a construction customer and a cleaning customer changes the workflow template, not the tool—so skill ramp faster and make fewer mistakes.

Reduced maintenance: Fixes and improvements to the core—call quality, scheduling reliability, reporting—ship to every segment at once. Reuse compounds instead of multiplying maintenance burden.

Decision 04 of 08

Customization by Segment

Most segment differences are configuration and template setup — not new engineering.

Aspect Construction Florist Cleaning
Custom Fields Site address, crew size, project name Arrangement type, colors, preferences Service checklist, team members
Pricing Template Labor + materials Arrangement-tier pricing Frequency discounts
Workflow Multi-day project cycle Fast quote → delivery Recurring + auto-invoice
Automation Weekly status updates Same-day fulfillment alerts Team assignment & route optimization

Configuration & Template Setup

Custom fields, pricing templates, intake scripts, and notification wording are configuration: data wired into the shared core. A new segment of this kind is a setup exercise, not a development project.

Genuinely New Subsystems

A few capabilities are real engineering: the Project Estimation engine, Seasonal Forecasting, Multi-Location Dispatch, and Route Optimization. These ship as paid add-on variants—built once, sold per segment—rather than as forks of the product.

Key distinction: Segment-specific = configuration. Variant-specific = new code. This separation keeps the backlog manageable and lets the team scale segments without proportional engineering growth.

The bundle math, illustrated: A Pro customer who attaches two variants—say Project Estimation ($199) and Multi-Location ($199)—pays $299 + $199 + $199 = $697/month, or $8,364/year. Variants more than double the value of a core subscription while reusing the same platform—the engine behind the margin story.

Unit economics insight: Year 1.5 break-even is feasible because variants have ~85% gross margin (core AI amortized). A small cohort of variant-paying customers can offset core platform R&D; as segments scale, margin stays strong.

Five offerings, one platform: each variant reuses the core and adds unique logic only where needed.

Reuse first, unique logic last: Every variant rides on the same AI Call Engine, scheduling, customer database, and integrations. Unique code exists only where a segment's economics demand it—estimation for construction, forecasting for florists, dispatch for cleaning. That discipline is what lets a small team ship five offerings without proportional complexity.

Decision 08 of 08

Shared Parts Architecture (DSM)

A design-structure view of the platform: how much of each layer is shared, and why that discipline limits variant sprawl.

Each layer defines what is reusable and what is segment or variant-specific. This prevents variants from drifting into forks.

✓ Whole Product (100% Shared)

Fully shared. Every customer, every segment, every variant runs on the same foundation.

Cloud Infrastructure
Authentication & Security
User Management
⊞ Major Assemblies (80% Shared)

Shared with segment-configuration. The assemblies are common; templates and rules vary per segment.

AI Call Engine
Scheduling Engine
Customer Database
Notification System
◆ Components (40% Shared)

Loosely coupled. Common wiring; segment-specific integrations and reporting.

CRM Integrations
Calendar Sync
Payment Processing
Reporting Dashboard
✗ Variant-Specific (0% Shared)

Built once per variant; sold as add-ons across segments where demand exists. No forking.

Project Estimation Engine
Seasonal Forecasting
Multi-Location Dispatch
Route Optimization

The dependency insight: Dependency ties downward: variant-specific modules depend on components, which depend on major assemblies, which depend on the whole product. Whole product is depended upon by everyone else. That hierarchy prevents variants from modifying core and forces discipline: if you need to change the AI Call Engine for one segment, you change it for all. If the change is segment-specific, build a variant, not a fork.

Result: One codebase. Minimal fork risk. Every customer and segment benefits from core fixes and improvements. Variants grow as add-ons, not branches.
